q: Coonawarra sits at 37°S yet drinks like a cool climate — give the mechanisms.
accept: latitude misleads ocean currents determine
maritime moderation trumps latitude numbers
ans: Latitude alone misleads — cold currents and maritime exposure make Coonawarra (37°S) cooler-acting than its number
exp: Always answer climate questions with mechanisms, not degrees.

q: Name three canopy-management levers and the wine consequence of each.
accept: leaf removal shoot thinning hedging crop thinning
leaf pull sun exposure shoot positioning airflow hedging vigor
ans: Leaf removal (fruit-zone sun/air → color, less pyrazine), shoot thinning (vigor balance), hedging/trimming (redirect energy), crop thinning (concentration)
exp: Every tasting deduction about 'green' or 'sunburnt' traces to these.

q: Name four viticultural adaptations to warming and one drawback of each.
accept: altitude aspect rootstock varieties canopy irrigation cost limits
higher sites late varieties shading rootstocks
ans: Higher/cooler sites (cost, frost), later-ripening varieties (market resistance), drought rootstocks (vigor trade-offs), canopy shading and later picking (labor, disease risk)
exp: Every adaptation buys years, not permanence.

q: Explain how vine age interacts with drought years, mechanistically.
accept: deeper roots access subsoil water buffer stress old vines cope
root depth reserves
ans: Established deep roots reach subsoil moisture and stored carbohydrate reserves buffer stress — old vines ripen more evenly in drought while young vines shut down
exp: Why 2003 and 2022 separated old-vine bottlings from the rest.

q: Explain how you would evaluate a new vineyard site from scratch.
accept: climate data soil pits water availability aspect slope frost risk market
site survey approach
ans: Long-run climate data and degree days, soil pits for depth and drainage, water availability and rights, aspect and slope, frost and hail history — then market access and what will actually sell
exp: The last clause is what separates a Master from an enthusiast.

q: Compare the chalk of Champagne with the limestones of the Cote d'Or as growing media — composition, water behaviour, and what each does to the vine.
accept: cretaceous chalk porous with a water reserve versus jurassic hard limestone and marl banded down a slope
champagne chalk holds water in micropores keeps roots cool high ph cote dor is thin stony limestone and marl varying with slope position
chalk is an even sponge the cote dor varies vertically with soil depth and clay limestone ratio
ans: Champagne sits on Cretaceous chalk, the belemnite and micraster beds, hundreds of metres thick, soft enough to dig cellars into and around 30-40% porous. It behaves like a sponge with drainage: excess water passes through, but an enormous reserve is held in micropores that roots and capillary rise draw on right through a dry summer, so the vine rarely suffers acute stress. It keeps the root zone cool and runs at high pH, which is where the lime-tolerant rootstock question comes from. The Cote d'Or is Jurassic and layered: hard Bathonian and Bajocian limestones — Comblanchien, Premeaux — interbedded with Argovian and Oxfordian marls, then reworked downslope as scree and colluvium. The result is thin, stony, sharply drained soil mid-slope, heavier marl and clay at the top of the slope and again on the flat below. So chalk gives evenness across a gentle landscape — the variable there is grower and village more than metre-by-metre soil — while the Cote's variation is vertical: soil depth, clay-to-limestone ratio and slope position change every fifty metres, which is exactly why its classification is a narrow strip and not a zone. Caveat the answer: Champagne's chalk is only near the surface on the Cote des Blancs and parts of the Montagne, while the Vallee de la Marne runs to clay, marl and sand, and the Cote des Bar is Kimmeridgian marl — the same bed as Chablis.
exp: Both are high-pH calcareous, both are classified, but for different reasons — and a Master answer says why the classifications look so different on a map. The Cote's ranking tracks slope position and soil depth; Champagne's crus were a price scale for grapes across broad villages. Mention the Kimmeridgian link between the Aube and Chablis and you have shown you know the geology crosses appellation borders.

q: Trace the ideal water regime of a red-wine vineyard through the season, stage by stage, and say what too much and too little does at each.
accept: full water early then a mild progressive deficit from set to veraison held steady never severe
gentle water deficit after set makes small berries and phenolics rain at harvest dilutes and splits
regulated deficit irrigation mimics a stony soil over a reserve shoot growth should stop at veraison
ans: Budbreak to flowering the vine should have a full profile and no stress at all: it is building the canopy that will ripen the crop, so drought here costs you the engine, while waterlogging suffocates roots and invites disease. At flowering and set, gentle steady supply — severe stress causes coulure and millerandage, and so does runaway vigour, because a shoot still growing hard competes with the flower for assimilates. Set to veraison is the window that makes the wine: a mild, progressive deficit slows and then stops shoot growth, redirecting assimilate to the fruit, holding berries small so the skin-to-pulp ratio rises, and triggering abscisic acid signalling that pushes anthocyanin and tannin synthesis in the skin. Veraison to harvest, hold that mild deficit steady — a hard stress now closes stomata, halts sugar loading and leaves you with unripe tannin under rising alcohol as the berry dehydrates, while rain now swells berries, dilutes, splits skins and opens the door to botrytis. So the shape is: full early, an early and gentle deficit, never severe, never relieved by a flood. That is precisely what a stony, free-draining topsoil over a clay, chalk or deep-rooting reserve delivers on its own, and what regulated deficit irrigation tries to buy where the soil will not provide it. The field test is simple and worth saying: shoot growth should have stopped by veraison. Tips still growing means the vine is still choosing leaves over fruit.
exp: This is the single most useful mechanistic frame in viticulture, because it converts vague soil talk into a testable sequence. Note the asymmetry that trips people: the damage from stress is stage-dependent, so the same soil moisture reading is excellent in July and disastrous in May. And note that severe late stress produces a wine that is simultaneously high in alcohol and green in tannin — the profile people wrongly call over-ripe.

q: A guest asks whether the slate in the glass is really the slate in the ground. Answer as the science stands.
accept: no direct mineral transfer soil acts through water nitrogen vigour and temperature
minerality tracks acidity ph and sulfur compounds not dissolved rock
soil matters indirectly by setting vine stress nitrogen and ripeness not by flavour transfer
~no demonstrated pathway
~no direct mineral transfer
~no pathway by which rock minerals
ans: Not directly. There is no demonstrated pathway by which rock minerals become flavour: the ions the vine takes up — potassium, calcium, magnesium, iron — occur in wine at concentrations well below sensory threshold and are largely taste-neutral anyway, and repeated attempts to link soil geology to specific aroma compounds have found no transfer mechanism. What soil actually does is indirect and completely decisive. It sets water supply and drainage, and therefore vine stress and berry size. It sets nitrogen availability, which drives yeast-assimilable nitrogen, ferment health, thiol expression and whether a wine finishes clean or reductive. It sets root-zone temperature and, through colour and stone content, the mesoclimate at the fruit. It sets vigour, and vigour sets canopy density, shading and pyrazine retention. Those variables determine ripeness, acidity, pH and aromatic profile, which is everything we taste. Meanwhile what tasters call minerality maps onto measurable things: high acidity and low pH, low alcohol, reductive sulfur compounds and struck-match volatiles, sometimes a saline perception driven by pH and specific salts. So the honest answer is that slate does not put slate in the glass, but Mosel slate reliably makes a wine that tastes the way we mean when we say slate — through water, warmth, nitrogen and vigour rather than through the rock's own flavour. Denying terroir is as wrong as claiming stones taste.
exp: This question separates the Master from the enthusiast, because it demands you defend terroir while conceding the folk mechanism is false. Two details that earn credit: low-nitrogen sites — often the thin, stony, famous ones — tend to give reductive, struck-flint ferments, which is a soil effect arriving through the yeast, not the rock; and blind studies on soil-type identification in wine have never produced the clean result the romantic account requires.

q: Explain the decoupling of sugar and phenolic ripeness under warming, and the levers a grower and a winemaker actually have.
accept: sugar rises with heat while colour tannin and pyrazine ripeness lag and stall above thirty degrees
technological ripeness outruns phenolic ripeness so you pick early and adjust or wait and lose acid
heat accumulates sugar faster than phenolics mature levers are site variety canopy pruning date and picking
ans: Sugar accumulation is heat-driven and accelerates in warm conditions; the other ripening processes run on slower, partly independent clocks and are actively inhibited by heat. Anthocyanin synthesis stalls and existing pigment degrades above roughly 30-35C, tannin polymerisation and seed lignification take the time they take, and methoxypyrazine degradation depends on light and time in the fruit zone. Add heat-driven respiration of malic acid and the collapse of acidity, and the vintage arrives at 14.5% potential alcohol with green seeds, unresolved tannin and a pH of 3.8. Wait for the phenolics and you are at 16% with no acid left. That is the decoupling: technological ripeness outruns phenolic ripeness, and picking becomes a choice between two kinds of unripeness. Vineyard levers: cooler sites, higher elevation, north-facing and east-facing aspects; later-ripening varieties, clones and rootstocks; late pruning, which is the most studied single tool for pushing the whole cycle into cooler weeks and can move harvest by one to two weeks; higher trunks and canopy architecture that shades the fruit through the afternoon rather than stripping leaves; cover crops and no-till to keep soil cooler and hold water; and reduced cropping only where it will not accelerate sugar further. Cellar levers: pick earlier and extract more gently, use whole bunch and stems for freshness and pH buffering, cool ferments and shorter macerations, blend fractions picked on different dates, acidify where legal, and use reverse osmosis or spinning cone to remove alcohol if you are willing to admit it. Every one is a mitigation that buys years, not a reversal.
exp: The exam trap is calling a hot vintage 'riper'. It is often less ripe phenologically at a higher alcohol, which is why hot vintages so frequently taste simultaneously jammy and green. Two specifics worth naming: anthocyanin degradation above the mid-30s is why very hot years give paler, browner reds despite thick skins, and late pruning works because it delays budbreak and every subsequent stage, shifting veraison into shorter, cooler days.

q: Explain 'apical dominance' and one training system that exploits it.
accept: top buds suppress lower cane arching gobelet
hormonal priority of end buds arcure
ans: End buds hormonally suppress lower ones; cane-arching (arcure) and head-training redistribute vigor along the cane
exp: Mosel's heart-shaped single-pole training is applied hormone theory.

q: Rootstock chess: name one high-vigor and one drought/lime-tolerant classic.
accept: 110r 41b so4 1103p riparia gloire low
41b limestone 110r drought riparia devigorating
ans: e.g., high-vigour: SO4 or Kober 5BB (1103P runs vigorous too); drought: 110R/1103P; limestone/chlorosis: 41B — Champagne's choice; Riparia Gloire the classic devigorator
exp: Rootstock is terroir's silent partner; Masters name them like clones.

small wild ferment starter added to main tank
ans: A small pre-harvest wild-ferment starter used to seed the main tanks safely
exp: The natural-wine answer to stuck-ferment fear.

q: Carbonic vs semi-carbonic in Beaujolais practice:
accept: whole berry co2 intracellular vs partial crush juice ferment
full co2 sealed vs juice at bottom starts
ans: True carbonic: sealed CO2, intracellular fermentation in intact berries; semi-carbonic (the real norm): bottom berries crush, ferment, blanket the rest
exp: Intracellular fermentation markers: kirsch (benzaldehyde), banana (isoamyl acetate), and lift — malic acid degraded and amino acids metabolised inside the intact berry.

cleaning beeswax oxidation skin tannin balance
ans: Porous-wall hygiene (beeswax linings, sulfur candles) and oxidative/phenolic overreach during long macerations
exp: Georgia's 8,000-vintage résumé notwithstanding, the vessel forgives nothing.

draining tank off skins returning over cap
ans: Rack-and-return: draining the fermenting must entirely off the cap, then pouring it back over
exp: Aggressive-but-gentle extraction plus seed removal — the paradox explained aloud.
